What dates and penalties apply to Christian County bills?

State law fixes them. KRS 134.015 allows a 2 percent discount for full payment through November 1, charges the printed amount through December 31, adds 5 percent during January and 10 percent afterward.

The sheriff's fees ride on top. The Department of Revenue's worked example shows a $1,000 bill reaching $1,254 on the day it moves to the clerk: a $100 penalty, a $110 add-on fee and a $44 commission, using an assumed 4 percent rate. If your house lies inside Hopkinsville, Oak Grove or another city, ask that city whether it bills its own tax and on what dates.

Landlords gain the most from early payment, since 2 percent on several rentals adds up. If a servicer or property manager pays your bill, confirm each year that the payment was made.

How do I dispute a Christian County assessment?

Schedule a conference with the Christian County PVA while the roll is open for public review. The PVA must explain how your number was reached, and a telephone conference is allowed if you ask.

Without a deal, deliver a written appeal to the county clerk the workday after the review period ends. A local board meets about a month later and weighs comparable sales, contracts, insurance policies and, for rentals, income and expense statements. Anyone paid to speak for you must be an attorney, accountant, tax consultant, broker, appraiser or your own employee, and must carry your written authority.

  • The board can raise a value as well as lower it, so bring evidence for your number.
  • The state's tax appeals board hears later appeals, though only from owners who first used the county board.
  • Payment on the value you claim stays due while the appeal runs.

When does the Christian County delinquent tax sale happen?

The clerk holds it once a year in summer. The county website set the sale for July 28, 2026, starting at 9:00 am Central, and asked participants to register by close of business on July 20, 2026. Both dates are past, and the next sale will follow a similar schedule.

A state timetable sits behind it. Unpaid bills transfer to the clerk on April 15, and a county sale has to fall between 90 and 135 days after that transfer. In the meantime the county attorney mails notices and the clerk advertises the list at least 30 days ahead. A buyer who wants more than three bills in the county, or more than five statewide, must register with the Department of Revenue 60 days before the sale.

Paying beforehand ends the matter. Paying afterward means dealing with the new lien holder.

Who qualifies for the homestead exemption in Christian County?

Owners aged 65 and up, or totally disabled, living in the home. Revenue lists the deduction at $49,100 for 2025 and 2026, taken from the assessed value before tax is figured. Apply at the Christian County PVA with proof of age or disability. Disability claims renew each year, except for veterans with service-connected disabilities and owners with permanent findings from Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

Ask the PVA how a move, or renting the house out, affects the exemption before you change how the property is used.

How can I sell a Christian County house that owes tax?

Collect payoff figures first and price with them in mind. The sheriff's tax office can state a current balance, and the clerk can say whether an earlier year was filed as a delinquency. The title company subtracts both at closing and records the release.

Moves tied to Fort Campbell can leave little time, and penalties keep running on the statutory dates. A purchaser willing to take the house without repairs can close on your date and clear the tax from your proceeds, which beats catching up in cash while you pack. Ask any buyer to show how the tax payoff and lien release will be handled on the closing statement before you agree to a price.

The clerk is at 511 South Main Street, Hopkinsville, KY 42240, phone (270) 887-4105, on weekdays between 8:00 am and 4:00 pm. The legal records division is at (270) 887-4109.

The county website scheduled it for July 28, 2026 at 9:00 am Central, with registration due July 20, 2026. Both dates are behind us.

What happens to a Christian County tax bill after April 15?

The bill moves from the sheriff to the county clerk as a certificate of delinquency, and a lien attaches to the parcel. Interest of 1 percent a month and clerk and attorney fees are then added.

Do I still owe tax if a renter lives in my Christian County house?

Yes. Property tax is the owner's personal debt from the assessment date, no matter who occupies the house.

Can a Christian County owner past 65 reduce the tax?

Yes, through the homestead exemption, which was $49,100 for 2025 and 2026. Apply at the Christian County PVA and show proof of age.

Who bills and collects Carter County property tax?

Three courthouse offices split the job in Carter County. The Property Valuation Administration puts a value on each parcel, the county clerk prints the bills and inherits the unpaid ones, and the sheriff takes payments through the autumn and winter. You will find all three at 300 West Main Street in Grayson, so one visit can settle most questions.

The county is a long stretch of northeastern Kentucky with about 412 square miles of land and water. Greenup and Lawrence counties gave up the ground for it in 1838. Grayson is the seat and Olive Hill is the only other city, which means most of the 12,206 housing units counted in 2020 are rural parcels, farm tracts and older frame houses billed as county property.

Where do I go for Carter County tax questions?

Start with the office that matches the question: value goes to the PVA, a bill amount or payment goes to the sheriff, and anything already delinquent goes to the clerk. The county's official directory lists the details below.

Carter County offices that handle property tax (county officials page)
OfficeAddressPhoneHours listed
Property Valuation Administration300 West Main Street, Suite 214, Grayson(606) 474-5663Mon to Fri 8:30 am to 4:00 pm; last Saturday of the month 8:30 am to noon
Sheriff (tax collection)300 West Main Street, Grayson(606) 474-5616Mon to Fri 8:30 am to 4:00 pm; last Saturday of the month 8:30 am to noon
County Clerk (tax bills, delinquent taxes)300 West Main Street, Grayson(606) 474-5188Mon to Fri 8:30 am to 4:00 pm; Grayson office open the last Saturday of each month, Olive Hill office open Saturdays 8:00 am to noon

The county site also lists an Olive Hill clerk location with its own Saturday hours.

What kind of houses and neighborhoods does Carter County have?

Mostly owner-occupied homes outside town limits, many of them decades old. The 2020 census found 10,664 households, with 75.7 percent of occupied units owned and 12.6 percent of all units empty. Only about one resident in five lived in an area the census treats as urban. The county population was 26,627 in 2020 and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 26,149.

The landscape explains the housing. A through rail route between Lexington and Ashland, later the Chesapeake & Ohio line, reached the county in 1881, and fire clay and refractory brick plants at Olive Hill and Hitchins were major industries in the early and mid 1900s. The Olive Hill depot, built in 1910, is on the National Register of Historic Places. Today Interstate 64 and US 60 carry traffic through the county, and the Carter County School District runs the public schools.

  • Carter Caves State Resort Park lies inside the county line.
  • Kentucky Christian University is in Grayson.
  • Adjoining counties are Greenup, Boyd, Lawrence, Elliott, Rowan and Lewis.

What do Carter County owners pay, and when?

The statewide calendar in KRS 134.015 governs. Your bill arrives near the start of October, and the total you owe depends on the day you pay.

  • Through November 1, a full payment earns 2 percent off.
  • From November 2 to year end, the printed amount is due.
  • All of January adds a 5 percent penalty.
  • Once February begins, the penalty becomes 10 percent and the sheriff's add-on fee applies.

The law treats the tax as your personal debt from the assessment date, and a lien on the land lasts eleven years no matter who buys it. Call the sheriff at (606) 474-5616 if a bill does not show up, and ask that office how it accepts mailed or in-person payments.

How can a Carter County owner contest a valuation?

Begin with the PVA, because Kentucky makes a conference there the entry ticket to every later step. The state opens each county's roll to the public for thirteen days from the first Monday of May, and the conference has to take place before or during that window.

If talking to the PVA does not move the number, deliver a written petition to the county clerk by the next workday after the window closes. Say which parcel is involved and what you think it would fetch on the open market. A local board then hears the case roughly a month later. It looks for proof, such as sale listings, construction costs and insurance policies, and it denies petitions that come without any. Owners who skip the board lose the right to go on to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals.

Filing never stops the clock on payment. You owe tax on the figure you claimed until the case ends, and a higher final value brings a supplemental bill.

What happens to Carter County bills still unpaid in mid-April?

They leave the sheriff and land on the county clerk's desk on April 15. Each one becomes a certificate of delinquency, and the clerk reports that totals jump by about 40 percent once the added charges are counted. Personal checks do not work for these bills, while cash, money orders, company checks and cards (with a user fee) do.

The clerk will sometimes arrange a payment plan: a third of the balance up front and the remainder within 90 days. Miss the deadline and the bill returns to the delinquent list, and the money already paid is kept and credited rather than refunded.

  • The clerk places an ad about 30 days ahead of the sale and posts the list online.
  • The sale for 2024 bills took place August 29, 2025, at 10 am in the fiscal courtroom.
  • Bidders sign up at least ten days beforehand, and the lien assignment fee is $46.

A successful bidder gets the right to collect from you, so settling before April 15 is far cheaper.

Which Carter County owners get a homestead break?

Retirees and owners with a total disability who live in the house they own. The state takes a fixed sum off the assessed value before it applies the rate, and the sum stood at $49,100 for the assessment years 2025 and 2026. On a house assessed at $120,000, the taxable portion would shrink to $70,900. Apply at the Carter County PVA, which also knows the current figure, since it is reset every second year.

A birth certificate, driver's license or passport proves age. Disability applicants renew yearly, with exceptions for veterans with a service-connected rating and owners found permanently disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

How do I sell a Carter County house that still owes tax?

Yes, you can, because the title company pays the balance out of your price. First ask the sheriff for a payoff on this year's bill and ask the clerk whether any older year was filed as delinquent. A recorded certificate appears in a title search and must be paid or released for the buyer to receive clear title.

Timing matters. A bill still with the sheriff carries only the 5 or 10 percent penalty, while one at the clerk adds fees and interest. When the house is inherited, vacant or short on repairs, a cash purchaser that takes it as it stands can settle the tax from your proceeds, so you do not have to bring money to the table.

More questions about Carter County, KY Property Tax Guide

Which office takes Carter County property tax payments?

The sheriff, at 300 West Main Street in Grayson, phone (606) 474-5616. Bills that go unpaid past April 15 are handled by the county clerk.

What if my Carter County tax bill never arrives?

Call the sheriff's office and give your name or parcel number. Ask how it takes payments by mail, and confirm the address before you send a check.

How late can I file a Carter County assessment appeal?

The petition goes to the clerk by the next workday after the May inspection window closes. A conference with the PVA must come first.

Will the Carter County clerk accept my personal check on a delinquent bill?

No. The clerk's page says personal checks are refused on delinquent bills and lists cash, money orders, company checks and cards instead. Card payments carry a user fee.

Can I list my Carter County house while back taxes are open?

Yes. The payoff is taken from your proceeds at closing, so get written balances from the sheriff and the clerk before you sign a contract.

What kind of place is Bracken County, Kentucky?

Bracken County is small and entirely rural, running along the Ohio River in the northern part of the state. Brooksville holds the courthouse, Augusta is the biggest town, and Germantown rounds out the three incorporated cities. Across the water lie Clermont and Brown counties in Ohio. On the Kentucky side the neighbors are Mason, Robertson, Harrison and Pendleton. Bracken falls inside the Cincinnati metro area, and it covers 209 square miles.

Kentucky made it the 23rd county in 1796 and named it for Big and Little Bracken creeks. The seat moved from Augusta to Woodward's Crossing, today's Brooksville, in 1833. White burley tobacco was bred from Bracken seed, and farm fields still define the landscape. The 2020 count was 8,400 residents, none of them in an urban area, and the July 2025 estimate stands at 8,511.

The Augusta area holds several Underground Railroad sites, because local abolitionists helped people cross the river to Ripley, Ohio, and Augusta College, founded in 1822, was the first Methodist college in the world.

When a value dispute arises, the sales records held at the PVA are what the county appeals board looks at.

What do Census numbers say about housing in Bracken County?

QuickFacts covers 2020 to 2024 for the figures below. Against Boyle, Breckinridge and Bullitt, Bracken has the cheapest typical home and the longest drive to work.

The 2020 count found 3,839 housing units, with 13.3 percent empty. Employers numbered 98 in 2023, and about 58.3 percent of residents 16 and older were in the labor force. Turnover is low: 95.7 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, the highest share of the four counties. The county counts 462 veterans, and broadband reaches 89.8 percent of households, and retail sales for 2022 totaled $29.6 million, or $3,506 per resident.

Who do I call about a Bracken County tax bill?

Valuing and collecting happen in separate offices that share the courthouse at 116 West Miami Street in Brooksville. The Property Valuation Administrator, 606-735-2228, owns the assessment, the property address, the name and mailing address on the bill, and exemptions. The Sheriff's Office (606-735-3233, second floor) only collects.

  • Address or name wrong: fix it on the return stub or call the PVA.
  • Disagree with the value: call the PVA before paying.
  • Bills from earlier years: County Clerk, 606-735-2952, on a separate check.

An online portal shows and takes payment for bills. Cards add a 2.50 percent charge that the cardholder pays and the sheriff does not keep. By mail, the check must cover the exact amount due.

When does the Bracken County discount end?

The sheriff gives the 2 percent discount period as October 1 through November 1. Bills go directly to owners. Later cutoffs and penalty steps are printed on the bill itself, and the sheriff's office can read them to you.

Escrow causes most of the grief. The sheriff mails to the owner and never to a mortgage company, so a borrower whose lender pays from escrow should pass the bill along as soon as it lands, or check that the lender has asked the sheriff for it. A check that bounces puts the bill back to unpaid, with the repayment schedule on the bill and a returned-check fee on top.

Why might a Bracken County bill carry the previous owner's name?

Ownership for tax purposes freezes on January 1. If a purchase closes after that, the bill for the year is addressed to the person who sold, and the PVA works from recorded deeds to find new owners. A buyer whose copy never turns up can ask the sheriff for one.

For a seller, that means a bill can show up at an address already left behind. The settlement agent normally divides the year by days of ownership and either pays the sheriff or credits whichever side will. Leave a forwarding address with the closing agent.

How does a Bracken County owner challenge an assessment?

Book a conference at the PVA first, since state rules require one before an appeal. The roll opens to inspection for thirteen days beginning with the first Monday of May, and appeals are filed with the clerk by the next workday after those days end.

If the PVA raises a value above what you listed, KRS 132.450(4) obliges the office to notify you. Anyone paid to speak for you must be an attorney, accountant, broker, appraiser or other qualified professional and must show your written authorization. Hearings may be recorded on audio.

What happens to an unpaid Bracken County bill after April 15?

The sheriff hands every unpaid bill to the County Clerk, who records a lien and files each as a certificate of delinquency. The clerk gives the Department of Revenue a list by May 15, and the Department publishes each county's list by June 1. On the normal schedule a tax sale can fall on any business day between July 14 and August 28.

Before that, the county attorney sends a 30-day letter and a second letter naming the sale date. The list is advertised in the paper with the biggest paid circulation between 30 and 45 days ahead and posted online at least 30 days ahead. An owner who still owes at the sale risks having the lien assigned to an outside buyer, who may add fees.

Interest accrues at 1 percent for every month or fraction. In the state's worked example, a $1,000 bill grows to $1,254 at transfer and to about $1,660 if paid after the June advertising.

Does Bracken County offer homestead relief?

Yes, to owners who turn 65 during the year or are permanently disabled. The Department of Revenue capped the exemption at $49,100 for tax years 2025 and 2026. The house must be your owned, occupied and maintained residence on January 1, and the application is due at the PVA by December 31.

The sheriff tells eligible owners to phone the PVA before paying a bill that lacks the exemption, because the exemption shrinks the bill. About 20.3 percent of Bracken residents are 65 or older.

How can I sell a Bracken County house that owes tax?

Treat the tax as a closing item. Get the present balance from the sheriff and any older balance from the clerk, and have the closing agent pay both from the proceeds. Inherited houses, houses with tenants and houses that need more work than a retail buyer will take on often sell to cash buyers who accept the property as it stands and pay the tax at the table.

606-735-2228, at the courthouse in Brooksville. The office handles assessments, mailing addresses on bills and homestead exemptions.

Where do I pay a Bracken County property tax bill?

At the sheriff's second-floor office in the courthouse, by mail, or through the sheriff's online portal. Card payments add 2.50 percent.

Does my mortgage company get my Bracken County tax bill?

No. The sheriff mails only to the owner. If your lender escrows taxes, forward the bill or ask the lender to request it.

Where do I pay a prior-year Bracken County bill?

At the County Clerk's office, 606-735-2952, with a separate check from the current year's payment.

Who owes tax on a Bracken County house sold in the spring?

The bill goes to whoever owned the house on January 1. Buyer and seller normally split the year at closing, and the agent pays the sheriff.

What should a Princeton seller know about how Caldwell County taxes a house?

The local Property Valuation Administrator values the house, the Caldwell County Sheriff collects the money, and anything unpaid after April 15 goes to the clerk. Values are fixed as of January 1, and the Department of Revenue says the PVA must walk every parcel at least once in four years, as described on its real property assessment page.

Princeton anchors a county of roughly 345 square miles of land. A Caldwell bill adds together several taxing districts, among them the state, the county and the schools, and each of those bodies picks its own rate. The assessor has no say over rates.

The county has long been farm country. Farmland is taxed on what it can produce rather than on market price. The sheriff's site says a parcel of ten or more acres used for livestock or crops, timber included, can qualify, so an owner with acreage should ask the PVA how the land is carried before listing.

Which dates and penalties apply to a Caldwell County tax bill?

The payment year runs on a fixed monthly ladder that starts on November 1 and ends on April 15. The sheriff's tax page lays out the steps, and the statewide framework behind them is KRS 134.015.

Collection for 2026 opened November 2, 2026, after bills were mailed October 30, and the sheriff replaced postcards with letter-style bills. Whatever the phase, a payment is credited if it is postmarked, handed over or dropped in the box before the next phase begins. The ladder looks like this:

  • All of November: the bill less 2%.
  • All of December: the bare face amount.
  • All of January: 5% extra.
  • February 1 through April 15: 21% extra.

The office is the first door to the right off Main Street inside the Princeton courthouse. It takes checks, money orders, cashier's checks, cash and, at the counter, cards with a processing surcharge. A drop box by the east courthouse door handles after-hours payments, with no cash allowed. Hours run 8 am to 4 pm on weekdays, and the sheriff posts a holiday closing list each season.

Which Caldwell County office answers which tax question?

Three numbers cover almost every question: 270-365-2088 for the sheriff, 270-365-7227 for the PVA and 270-365-6754 for the clerk. The PVA is on the courthouse's second floor at 100 East Market Street, and the sheriff takes mail at Room 25 of the same building.

  • Sheriff: mails bills, accepts payment until April 15, and runs a view-only bill search online.
  • PVA: sets values, takes homestead and disability forms, and holds the conference that must come before an appeal.
  • County clerk: takes over delinquent bills and records deeds.

The bill is addressed to whoever owned the parcel on January 1. A buyer whose bill went to the previous owner can print it from the sheriff's site, and the sheriff, who does not receive deed transfers, lists the new name in care-of form the first year.

How can a Princeton owner dispute a Caldwell County value?

Book a conference with the PVA first, then file at the clerk's office no later than the workday after public inspection ends. Inspection lasts 13 days from the first Monday in May, and the local appeals board sits up to five days beginning 25 to 35 days later, as the state property tax calendar explains.

Bring facts, not opinions. Useful evidence includes lot and building descriptions, insurance papers, what the house cost to build and listings of comparable sales. An appeal without that paper is denied. Skipping the local board also closes the door to later review. Because bills can print before a case ends, the value you claim is billed in the meantime, and a supplemental bill arrives if the board lands higher.

Whatever number survives is what a buyer's lender and title company will see. A Princeton owner whose house has gained a new roof or an addition should check that the PVA's record describes the house as it stands.

Which relief programs lower a Caldwell County bill?

Owner-occupants who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, can have part of the assessed value removed. The sheriff's page puts the maximum at $46,350 for 2024 and 2025, and KRS 132.810 resets it every two years, so the PVA can quote the current figure.

Applicants must live in the house they own, prove their age and claim no exemption elsewhere. The form is completed at the PVA office, which the sheriff says takes under five minutes. The benefit stays with the owner, so whoever buys from you files separately.

An older seller should confirm the exemption shows on the bill before closing. The sheriff asks owners to sort out a missing exemption with the PVA before paying.

What happens to the Caldwell County bill at closing?

The lien stays with the parcel while the closing agent splits the year between the two sides. According to the sheriff's FAQ, your agent or lender explains the split, since the sheriff is never told how a sale handled it.

Unpaid bills stay alive after a sale. Delinquent bills move to the clerk with penalties and 1% monthly interest, as the Department of Revenue's collection process page shows. A Princeton owner with back taxes should get the clerk's payoff figure before picking a closing date.

Where a lender escrows taxes, the bill still goes to the owner, and the sheriff says forwarding it is the owner's job. Checking in with the servicer now and then keeps a missed forward from becoming a penalty.

Caldwell County has about 12,600 residents, and its typical owner-occupied home is valued at $118,500 for 2020 to 2024, far under Campbell County in northern Kentucky. Princeton, with 6,270 people in 2020, grew up around railroad junctions. It hosts a University of Kentucky research campus, factories such as Bremner provide jobs, and a December 2021 tornado hit the south side of town.

Roughly 30 percent of occupied homes here are rentals, and 93.4 percent of residents had not moved in the past year, so few houses change hands. Those that do often belong to estates, older owners or farm families, and an owner facing repairs or a tenant may prefer a direct cash sale to skip showings.

What dates matter for Caldwell County tax bills?

The bill opens for payment on November 1, and the 2% discount lasts through November 30. December is face value, January adds 5% and February 1 to April 15 adds 21%. Anything still open on April 15 goes to the county clerk.

Where can I pay a tax bill in Princeton?

Go to the sheriff's office in the courthouse, mail to 100 E. Market St., Room 25, or use the drop box at the east door. The website search only displays bills, and phone payments are not taken.

Which Clay County offices deal with property tax?

Clay County splits the job three ways. The Property Valuation Administrator decides what a parcel is worth, the Sheriff prints and collects the bills, and the County Clerk takes appeal papers and later inherits any bill the sheriff could not collect. Knowing which desk owns which question saves a seller several wrong-number calls.

All three share one building, 102 Richmond Road in Manchester. The PVA sets no tax rate and accepts no payments. Its work ends at the number on the roll.

Clay County property tax contacts (source: Clay County Fiscal Court department pages and county clerk site)
OfficeHandlesReach it
Property Valuation AdministratorValuation, exemptions, ownership changesSuite 200, 606-598-3832, Monday to Friday, closing at 4:30
SheriffTax bills and collectionSuite 100, 606-598-3471
County ClerkAppeal filings, unpaid-bill certificates, deed recordingSuite 101, 606-598-2544

What is Clay County like for someone selling a house?

Clay County sprawls across 471 square miles of Appalachian hills with Manchester at its center. Kentucky created it in 1807 from land that belonged to Floyd, Knox and Madison, and named it for Green Clay. A fire took the courthouse in January 1936. Seven counties touch its borders: Owsley, Perry, Leslie, Bell, Knox, Laurel and Jackson. The Census Bureau groups Clay with the Corbin micropolitan area.

The 2020 count was 20,345 people. The July 2025 estimate is 19,465, which is 4.3 percent fewer, so a listing draws from a shrinking local pool. Census QuickFacts add this detail:

  • 7,288 households living in 8,781 housing units
  • 76.4 percent of households own their home
  • Typical home value: $90,700
  • Typical rent: $724 a month
  • Typical monthly owner cost: $978 with a mortgage, $367 without

A seller pricing near $90,700 will notice any unpaid tax in the final settlement figure.

How does the Clay County PVA decide what a house is worth?

Valuation is pegged to January 1. Kentucky wants fair cash value, which means the price a voluntary sale between informed parties would produce. Staff walk every parcel at least once in each four-year stretch, and new buildings join the roll every year.

A purchase can simplify things. When you bought in the previous year, the deed price may serve as next January's value, so long as nothing about the building changed. Frankfort values four categories itself: public service companies, bank shares, omitted tangible property and vehicles. Everything else, real and personal, belongs to the local PVA.

What else does the Clay County PVA keep track of?

Beyond the annual value, the office follows ownership changes, maintains parcel maps, updates building details and administers exemptions on real estate. A seller can ask the staff whether the map shows the correct acreage, whether the building record lists a finished basement or an outbuilding that no longer stands, and whether the exemption on file still matches the owner.

Errors in those records flow straight into the bill. Suppose a garage came down years ago but still sits on the record: it keeps lifting the value until someone asks for a correction. Visit during open hours, 8:00 to 4:30 on weekdays, or write to the office at 102 Richmond Road, Suite 200, Manchester, KY 40962.

When does a Clay County tax bill come due?

Collection follows Kentucky's fall-to-spring pattern, and the sheriff runs it. The Sheriff's page on the Fiscal Court website carries a View Property Tax Bill button for parcel lookups. The sheriff's office, at 606-598-3471, can confirm the exact opening date, since the state lets a county use 30-day phases when a different calendar is needed.

The state's typical pattern:

  • October 1 to November 1: 2 percent off
  • November 2 to December 31: face amount
  • January: 5 percent added
  • February 1 to April 15: 21 percent added

Because value is fixed on January 1, a bill may carry a previous owner's name after a sale made later in the year.

What is the route for contesting a Clay County valuation?

The sequence is fixed, and missing one step closes the door.

  • Look for the notice the PVA mails after raising a value.
  • Request a conference with the PVA or a deputy while the tax roll is open for inspection. That window starts the first Monday of May and covers two weeks, Monday through Saturday.
  • If talks fail, file the appeal paper with the County Clerk by close of business the next workday after the window ends.
  • Attend the local board hearing, held 25 to 35 days after inspection. The board gets five sitting days unless the state grants more.
  • Bring proof: sales of similar houses, an appraisal, or building costs. With no facts, the board has to deny you.

Filing and then failing to appear forfeits the right to continue. A dissatisfied owner can carry the case to the Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals.

Does Clay County give a homestead exemption?

It does, to people who live in the house and are at least 65 or are classified as totally disabled. For assessment years 2025 and 2026 the amount is $49,100, taken off the valuation before tax is figured. A home worth the county's typical $90,700 would be taxed on $41,600.

Apply at the PVA office in Manchester, 606-598-3832. Age is shown with a driver's license, birth certificate or passport. A disability claim needs paperwork from the federal agency or retirement system that made the classification. Most disability claims renew annually. Exceptions cover veterans with a service-connected disability and owners ruled permanently disabled by Social Security or Kentucky Retirement Systems.

What happens to an unpaid Clay County bill?

When business closes on April 15, the sheriff hands the bill to the County Clerk. It becomes a certificate of delinquency and a lien on the parcel. Interest of 1 percent per month begins, and the clerk adds 10 percent while the county attorney adds 20 percent.

The county attorney writes to owners in May and, if necessary, June, and can arrange installments. From mid-July, certificates may be sold to outside buyers through late October. After a sale you owe the buyer, and more fees follow. The Clay County Clerk's website posts a delinquent tax page for each year.

Where can a Clay County seller look up records online?

The Fiscal Court website, claycountyky.com, has a page for each department with contact details and hours. The sheriff's page holds the bill lookup. The County Clerk's own site lists Recordings, Fees, Forms and an Open Records Request page, along with a delinquent tax page for each year, which is the place to check whether a parcel was advertised for sale.

How do I handle the tax bill when I sell in Clay County?

The closing agent normally pays the current bill out of your proceeds and splits it with the buyer. An open delinquency has to be settled first, because the lien stays with the parcel. Get a payoff amount from the sheriff before signing a contract, and ask the PVA whether an exemption on the parcel ends when ownership changes.

The deed adds a separate charge. Kentucky taxes the seller $0.50 for every $500 slice of the price, and a partial slice counts in full. The clerk takes it at the recording counter. A $90,700 price makes 182 slices, so the charge is $91. Foreclosure deeds, divorce transfers, correction deeds and nominal gifts between parent and child fall outside the tax.

More questions about Clay County, KY Property Tax Guide

Who mails the Clay County tax bill?

The Sheriff does. If nothing arrives, call 606-598-3471 or use the bill lookup on the sheriff's page of the Fiscal Court site.

Can a Clay County owner contest a value in summer?

Generally no. Both the conference and the clerk filing must land in the May inspection window, with the filing due the next workday after it ends. Phone the PVA at 606-598-3832 in spring.

Does the Clay County PVA take tax payments?

No. That office only values property and processes exemptions. Money goes to the sheriff, then to the County Clerk after mid-April.

Is transfer tax owed on a Clay County sale?

Usually yes. The seller owes $0.50 per $500 of price, and the clerk collects it before recording. Foreclosure deeds, divorce transfers and correction deeds are exempt.

Can a Clay County house with a delinquent bill still be sold?

Yes. The delinquency gets paid at or before closing. Ask the County Clerk for the total with interest and fees so the title company can build it into the payoff.

What makes Carroll County, Kentucky, different for a house seller?

Carroll County is a small river county where the Kentucky River meets the Ohio, and its seat, Carrollton, sits at that confluence. At 128.68 square miles of land it is the third-smallest county in Kentucky by area, and the 2020 Census counted 10,810 residents. Carrollton lies about 54 miles from Cincinnati and 55 from Louisville along U.S. 42, with Interstate 71 about four miles south of town.

That location shapes who buys here. The county's own website lists employers such as North American Stainless, CertainTeed and Kentucky Utilities, and describes General Butler State Resort Park, a 791-acre park, as a local draw. Jefferson Community College serves the county. A house in Carrollton is often sold to a worker commuting along the river or I-71 corridor, and Carrollton itself was laid out in 1792 under the name Port William.

The city itself is compact, about two square miles with 3,890 residents in 2020. Prestonville lies across the Kentucky River to the west, and Switzerland County, Indiana, sits across the Ohio to the north. The county's own site adds that the Kentucky Veterans Memorial is in Carrollton and that boats launch from Point Park.

Carrollton's worst recorded flood was the Ohio River flood of 1937, with a crest of 79.9 feet, according to Wikipedia. Sellers of low-lying homes near the river should ask the city planning office for floodplain information.

Which Carroll County office does what with a tax bill?

A parcel is valued by the PVA, billed by the Sheriff's Office, and handed to the County Clerk if it goes delinquent. The county's clerk page lists those delinquent collections beside recording deeds and mortgages and filing wills and probate orders.

  • Sheriff: first floor of the courthouse at 440 Main Street, (502) 732-7010, with online tax lookup and payment through the sheriff's page.
  • County Clerk: same building, (502) 732-7005, for delinquent taxes and deeds.
  • County administration: (502) 732-5448, the office that edits or exonerates county tax amounts when a bill looks wrong.

Carroll's FAQ puts the annual due date at December 31 and expects bills in October or November. An owner who has seen nothing should look the bill up on the sheriff's page. In the state's description, most counties begin collecting on October 1 or November 1. The exact discount cutoff is printed on the bill, and the sheriff's office can confirm it.

Can Carroll County owners split payments or get a late fee waived?

Neither. The county FAQ rules out a payment plan and requires the whole bill in one transaction. It also says that a bill that never arrived is not a permitted ground for waiving late fees under the state's administrative regulations.

Mixing tender is fine, such as part check and part cash or card. The penalty ladder comes from KRS 134.015:

  • On or before the discount date: 2% off.
  • Until December 31: the printed amount.
  • During January: 5% on the unpaid tax.
  • Past January 31: 10%.

The debt also becomes a lien. A Carrollton house with a past-due bill will be flagged by the buyer's title company, so line up the clerk's payoff figure early.

How does a Carroll County tax sale work?

After April 15 the sheriff hands unpaid bills to the County Clerk, and a sale comes at least 90 days afterward. KRS 134.128, summarized on the state's collection page, puts the sale 90 to 135 days after the transfer, with notices to the owner at 30 and 60 days.

The clerk sold Carroll's 2025 delinquent taxes on July 24, 2026, at 9:30 a.m. on the courthouse's second floor, with third-party purchasers registering by July 14, 2026. Questions go to the clerk at (502) 732-7005. A buyer who purchases a certificate may add substantial fees, which is why owners fare better paying before the sale.

In the state's first example, a $1,000 bill paid within five business days of reaching the clerk costs about $1,388 once interest, a clerk commission and a recording fee are added. Waiting brings in the county attorney's commission, postage and advertising costs.

How can a Carrollton owner appeal a value?

Ask the PVA for a conference, then file with the clerk once the roll closes. The roll stays open 13 days after the first Monday in May, and an appeal is valid only after a conference with the PVA or a deputy, as the state calendar sets out.

The PVA must send notice whenever it assesses above the value you listed. A deed price can also serve as the listed value for the next January 1 if the property has not changed. For a Carroll County seller who bought recently, that means the purchase price may be the PVA's starting point, so keep your closing statement.

The local board owes a written explanation for any increase or decrease, and you may record the hearing. Do not skip it, since not filing or not appearing ends your right to further review.

Which exemptions are open to Carroll County homeowners?

The homestead exemption is available on a primary residence to owners aged 65 or more and to owners who are totally disabled. One state form, 62A350, covers both, and the PVA keeps it on file.

It deducts a set dollar amount from the assessed value, not the entire value, and the amount is reset every two years. A buyer cannot inherit it. Veterans with a total service-connected disability file once, as do owners found disabled by Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement System.

Ask the PVA for the current dollar amount, because the dollar figure published on the state's page covers a past assessment period. A seller who is 65 should confirm the exemption was applied before closing.

What do the numbers say about Carroll County homes?

A typical owner-occupied house in Carroll County is valued at $140,900 for 2020 to 2024, between Caldwell's $118,500 and Calloway's $183,200. Owners live in 65.7 percent of homes, the second-lowest share of the four counties, and the 2025 estimate of 11,141 residents is 3.1 percent above 2020.

The Census counted a single building permit in Carroll County in 2025, so most buyers are choosing among existing homes. Employers in Carroll County reported 6,600 jobs in 2023, with total payroll near $497 million, and employment rose 4.7 percent from 2022. Only 11.4 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree, and 17.3 percent of residents live in poverty, figures that sit beside the county's $140,900 median home value. Sellers who cannot wait for financing, or who are managing an estate or a rental with tenants, can sell as-is for cash and pay the tax payoff from the proceeds.

What is the Carroll County tax deadline?

December 31 is the annual due date, with a discount for bills paid by the early cutoff printed on your bill. January adds 5% and anything later adds 10%.

Does Carroll County allow a payment plan?

No. The county requires the full amount in a single transaction, though check, cash and card can be combined.

Whom do I call about delinquent Carroll County taxes?

The County Clerk, at (502) 732-7005, collects delinquent real estate taxes and runs the sale.

Is a late fee waived if my bill never came?

No. The county FAQ lists a missing bill as an impermissible reason for a waiver. Look the bill up on the sheriff's page each fall.

Can a Carrollton house with back taxes be sold?

Yes. A buyer can take it as-is and the payoff is paid from your proceeds at closing. Get the figure from the County Clerk before you sign.
